blocks.html: Today's long read: The wind man's second life - how Tulsi Tanti's Suzlon went from a Surat textile mill to the world's most valuable wind-turbine maker, through India's biggest bond default, and back to a record quarter. Read it here.
Wall Street's worst day since June: S&P 500 -2.30%, Nasdaq -3.57%, Dow -1.35%; Intel -28.6% on its guidance; Reddit -26%, Roblox -20%; money rotated into Exxon, Chevron, Mondelez and Colgate.
Reliance's record quarter: profit Rs 29,550 crore (+33.8%), record revenue and EBITDA; O2C earnings +68% on historic fuel cracks. Jio Platforms' first print: Rs 8,387 crore (+13.7%), ARPU Rs 218.8.

Mines in the Hormuz: three tankers struck, a fourth claimed by Iran's army - the first successful limpet-mine attack of the war; Houthis claim Ras Tanura; WTI settled $104.12, January Brent $113.43. Midterms Tuesday.
Binance's $6.3-billion hole: the largest crypto theft ever, four times the previous record; a North Korean unit the likely culprit; Bitcoin near $77,000.
India's quiet win: Sensex +308 to 74,460, a second straight gain while Asia bled; FIIs back with Rs 3,599 crore; records from BoB and IOC, a beat from BEL.

Suzlon's honest week: record deliveries and +26% revenue - and a margin-guidance cut, 17% to 15%; the stock fell 8%. The long read is the whole arc: leverage up, leverage down, and a second life built on discipline, with named people and dated events.

1. Day two of the AI reckoning: Intel sinks 29%, the Nasdaq loses 3.6%. Friday was Wall Street's worst day since June (AP, read in full): the S&P 500 fell 2.30% to 7,542.85, the Nasdaq Composite 3.57% to 25,248.82 and the Dow 1.35% to 51,634.35 - all end-of-day finals. Intel closed down 28.58% at $65.76 after guiding fourth-quarter revenue to $15-16 billion and GAAP earnings of $0.10 a share, below consensus - this from a stock that had risen about 250% this year and traded above 50 times 2027 earnings. The paradox at the centre: chief executive Lip-Bu Tan insisted AI-driven demand is "extremely high" while conceding PC headwinds; the market's verdict is that demand was never the question - financing is. Advanced Micro Devices and Marvell fell about 12%, Micron 7%, Nvidia 4.2% (the heaviest drag on the S&P, per AP) and the semiconductor ETF about 10%. Reddit fell 26% on weak user numbers and Google AI search eating its referral traffic; Roblox fell 20%. Amazon fell 1.9% after recovering from an early 6% drop - it has burned $42.4 billion of free cash flow over twelve months. The five biggest AI spenders have committed $800.6 billion of 2026 capital spending (BBC's accounting). The rotation was explicit: Exxon rose about 1.5%, touching a record intraday, after profit more than doubled to $15.4 billion; Chevron hit a record, Mondelez rose 3.7%, Colgate 3.2%. Gold fell 3% to $3,901.83, a one-year low - the safety bid went to Treasuries, where the ten-year yield completed its biggest monthly decline since late 2023, to about 4.92%. Cetera's Gene Goldman called it "a horror show... the real villain is AI spending"; Equity Armor's Joe Tigay named the regime change: from the "hopes and dreams phase" to the "show me phase." Editor's takeaway: two days, one message - the market now prices who funds the build-out, not who promises it. Watch Monday whether the cash printers keep the bid.

2. Reliance posts a record quarter - and Jio's first as a listed company. Reliance Industries' own media release (company release, via ril.com; Indian Express report) reads like a victory lap: record quarterly profit including associates and joint ventures of Rs 29,550 crore, up 33.8% year on year; record gross revenue of Rs 3,62,268 crore, up 27.8%; record EBITDA of Rs 62,409 crore, up 23.9%. The engine was oil-to-chemicals: O2C EBITDA rose 67.9% to Rs 25,203 crore as fuel cracks ran at three to 3.7 times year-ago levels - historic highs - and freight rates surged 15 to 20 times; the war's disruption is RIL's margin. Digital (Jio) EBITDA rose 17.7% to Rs 22,223 crore; Retail grew gross revenue 6.4% to Rs 91,716 crore but saw EBITDA fall 8.6%. Mukesh Ambani framed the moment around Wednesday's "record-setting" Jio listing and a "rejuvenation of the equity cult" from the 1977 Reliance IPO. Jio Platforms' first results since listing (Business Line, read in full): profit up 13.7% to Rs 8,387 crore on revenue up 11.4% to Rs 40,475 crore; EBITDA margin 54.1%; 542.4 million subscribers with 300 million on 5G; ARPU at Rs 218.8, up 3.5%. Managing director Akash Ambani sketched international expansion as a managed-services partner - "not a heavy capex rollout" - with investment in satcom, 6G intellectual property and AI-integrated services. Editor's takeaway: this is what funds-the-capex looks like - the week's American story in reverse, written in refinery margins.

3. Three tankers strike mines in the Hormuz - the war's first successful limpet attack. Three tankers struck mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, with a fourth reported by Iran's army, in the first successful limpet-mine strike in the waterway since the war began in February (AP, read in full; Reuters via maritime sources): a small boat attached two limpet mines to one hull, starting an engine-room fire; the UK's maritime agency confirmed explosive devices. One tanker carried more than two million barrels. The IRGC publicly rejected the US claim that lanes are cleared: "prove it with independent evidence." The same week, the Houthis claimed strikes on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura - the kingdom's largest refinery - plus Rabigh and Abqaiq; the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a cruise missile (CNBC, read in full). Diplomacy runs in parallel: Qatari mediators returned to Tehran Friday; Iran has received, not answered, a letter from Vice President Vance; the Wall Street Journal reports CENTCOM's chief presented military options Thursday with a strike window after Tuesday's midterms. Oil settled higher: WTI December at $104.12 (+$2.12) and January Brent at $113.43 (+$2.63) - the expired December Brent quoted near $117.64 late is a different contract; Brent gained about 14% in October, a fourth straight monthly rise. Exxon and Chevron cancelled executive travel to next week's ADIPEC show in Abu Dhabi. The standing conversion for your wallet: about $2 billion a year on India's import bill per dollar of crude - each $3 swing is a $6-billion annualized question. Editor's takeaway: mines in the water plus a vote on Tuesday means the premium holds into the election - and a signed deal remains the only thing that removes it at the root.

4. Binance loses $6.3 billion - the largest crypto theft in history. Binance confirmed a "security incident" that drained about $6.3 billion - four times the previous record, Bybit's $1.5 billion in February 2025 (AFP; Investopedia). A blockchain intelligence firm attributes the theft to a North Korean unit (AP). Withdrawals were suspended; Binance says all user losses will be covered, and co-CEO Richard Teng posted that the company is "recovering stolen assets for users." Founder Changpeng Zhao called it "a major disaster for the industry" - and told Elon Musk, who trolled the news, "Bad time to troll. Please stop." Binance.US says it is unaffected as a separate platform. Bitcoin fell about 3.7% to near $77,000, down from above $86,000 earlier in October; Coinbase fell 12.7% despite beating estimates, Robinhood 10%, Circle 11%, and Strategy 6% (its finance chief resigned for personal reasons the same day). FundStrat's Sean Farrell named the tell to watch: the resumption of withdrawals and whether outflows stay orderly. Editor's takeaway: in crypto, trust is the product - the exchanges that prove reserves fastest win the deposits that flee.

5. India climbs through the rout: records from Reliance, BoB and IOC, and the foreigners return. Indian equities posted a second straight gain while Asia bled (CNBC TV18; Business Standard and Economic Times close reports): the Sensex rose 308.49 points (0.42%) to 74,459.53 and the Nifty 116.35 points (0.51%) to 23,053.10, closing near the day's highs and finishing the week up 1.8% and 2% respectively. The Kospi fell 3.5%, the Nikkei 2.1% and Shanghai 1.4% on the same global tape - India outperformed because the bid is earnings-led. Foreign investors returned, buying a provisional Rs 3,598.54 crore, while domestic institutions sold Rs 817.51 crore - a clean reversal of Thursday's pattern. IT and pharma led (Wipro and Infosys topped the Nifty gainers); the Bank Nifty fell 223 points to 54,687 and midcaps fell 0.9%. The results slate delivered: Bank of Baroda a record Rs 6,532 crore profit (+36%), Indian Oil its best-ever quarter at Rs 21,630 crore, Bharat Electronics a beat at Rs 1,541 crore (+19.8%). Jio Platforms added 0.57% to Rs 1,431.20 in its third session. Editor's takeaway: one day is not a regime - but Friday's decoupling was bought with record profits, not hope.

Friday, the full picture. Sensex 74,459.53 (+0.42%), Nifty 23,053.10 (+0.51%), second straight gain, closing near the day's highs (CNBC TV18; ET and BS close reports). FIIs bought a provisional Rs 3,598.54 crore (bought Rs 20,564 crore, sold Rs 16,965 crore); DIIs sold Rs 817.51 crore. In New York overnight: S&P 500 7,542.85 (-2.30%), Nasdaq 25,248.82 (-3.57%), Dow 51,634.35 (-1.35%) - the worst day since June; the Nasdaq lost 2.7% on the week and is tracking its worst month since March 2025 (Investopedia). Asia Friday: Kospi -3.5%, Nikkei -2.1% (the Bank of Japan held, raising its inflation forecast; the yen gained a third day), Shanghai -1.4%, Hang Seng +1.5%. Europe was mixed: FTSE flat (AstraZeneca beat, BP strong), DAX -0.7%, NatWest -8%. Bonds rallied: the US ten-year at about 4.92%, from above 5.30% in early October - the biggest monthly yield decline since late 2023 (Reuters). Gold fell 3% to $3,901.83, a one-year low; silver fell 5.9% to $49.27, below $50 for the first time since November 2025.

blocks.html: What Monday watches. Four clocks: EAAA India Alternatives lists (band Rs 1,585-1,665, about 5.25 times subscribed); Jio Platforms begins its first full trading week at Rs 1,431.20, with all three broker targets below the price; the results slate continues into its final heavy week; and US futures reopen Sunday night India time with Tuesday's midterms priced at a 91-93% probability of a Democratic House. Above all: whether Friday's FII return (Rs 3,599 crore, provisional) survives the weekend's headlines.

Jio, day three: the quietest session yet - and the first results. Jio Platforms added 0.57% to Rs 1,431.20 on the BSE (Rs 1,431.30 on the NSE) - its calmest day since listing: +21.4% at the open on Wednesday, +0.40% Thursday, +0.57% Friday. It stands 27.9% above the Rs 1,119 issue price with a market value of Rs 13.18 lakh crore (The Hindu), India's second-largest listed company behind its own parent. The day's real Jio news was fundamental, not technical: its first quarterly results as a listed company - front page, item 2. The debut's superlatives stay on the record: a Rs 30,213-crore issue, subscribed 22.19 times with demand past Rs 7.4 lakh crore, fully covered in 100 minutes - the fastest mega-IPO in Indian history.

EAAA India Alternatives: listing Monday. The Edelweiss group's alternatives platform lists on Monday 2 November (band Rs 1,585-1,665, entirely an offer for sale, about 5.25 times subscribed overall - institutions 13 times, retail barely covered). Monday's open is the verdict on whether Jio's afterglow lifts the whole new-listing shelf or only the biggest name on it.
All figures are BSE official closing prints. Reasons traced to company releases or named reports; where no driver was confirmed, this paper says so rather than guess.

blocks.html: Gainers, with the why. Borosil (+19.98% to Rs 286.40): the day's standout, on its quarterly results on results day (ET/moneycontrol results blogs). Laurus Labs (+6.55% to Rs 2,392.00): quarterly results. Navin Fluorine International (+4.61% to Rs 8,676.35): quarterly results. Trent (+5.20% to Rs 3,015.10): the session's big large-cap gainer - no confirmed catalyst in the sources read. InterGlobe Aviation, IndiGo's parent (+4.06% to Rs 4,870.00): a supportive brokerage note (ET).

Losers, with the why. Suzlon Energy (-8.0% to Rs 33.85): the FY27 margin-guidance cut, 17% to 15%, announced with Thursday's record quarter - the full story is today's long read. Equitas Small Finance Bank (-6.26% to Rs 53.42): day two of the fallout from founder-CEO P N Vasudevan's resignation over the 'perception of conflict' involving his daughter's NBFC; the stock has now lost about 18% in two sessions. Coal India cooled after Thursday's results pop.

The beats. Reliance Industries: record profit Rs 29,550 crore (+33.8%), record revenue, record EBITDA - front page, item 2. Bank of Baroda: record profit of Rs 6,532 crore, up 36% year on year, with non-interest income up 95.8% to Rs 6,881 crore (helped by the NSE stake sale), net interest income up 9% to Rs 13,026 crore, a record operating profit of Rs 11,430 crore and gross NPAs down to 1.78% from 2.16% (The Hindu, read in full); management sees about Rs 7,000 crore of quarterly operating profit as sustainable. Indian Oil: its highest-ever quarterly standalone profit, Rs 21,630.03 crore - against a Rs 2,661-crore loss just last quarter and up 184% year on year - on refining margins, the temporary crude dip and LPG compensation (Business Line results blog). Bharat Electronics: profit up 19.8% to Rs 1,541 crore on revenue up 26.5% to Rs 7,291 crore, beating estimates, with an order book of Rs 68,717 crore. GAIL: standalone profit more than doubled to Rs 4,650.22 crore.

The misses - and the honest middle. Sun Pharmaceutical: consolidated profit fell 36% to Rs 1,989 crore on exceptional charges even as revenue rose 12% to Rs 16,199 crore; on a standalone basis profit rose 54.4% to Rs 871.3 crore - the two bases measure different things, and the consolidated figure carries the charges. Suzlon: comparable profit up just 1.3% to Rs 394 crore (the year-ago Rs 389 crore excludes a one-time tax credit; the reported figure was Rs 1,279 crore) with margin at 14.8% versus 18.6% - and the guidance cut that defined its week (long read). Dixon Technologies' profit fell; Zee's consolidated profit dipped to Rs 45.6 crore. Aditya Birla Capital's standalone profit rose 35%.

Dates for the diary. EAAA India Alternatives lists Monday 2 November. Infosys's Rs 26 interim dividend has its record date on Tuesday 3 November (payout 11 November). Coal India's Rs 10.25 interim has its record date on Wednesday 4 November (payment by 27 November). Tech Mahindra's postal ballot on a 1:1 bonus issue remains in voting - no record date has been set. HUL's Rs 19 interim record date falls Thursday 12 November (payment 25 November).

1. Cash flow is the new scoreboard. In two sessions the market repriced the AI trade by one metric: who funds themselves. The burners were destroyed - Alphabet $500 billion of value on Thursday, Intel 28.6% on Friday, Amazon carrying a $42.4-billion twelve-month free-cash-flow burn. The printers were bid up - Exxon touching a record (profit more than doubled to $15.4 billion), Chevron hitting one, Mondelez (+3.7%), Colgate (+3.2%). The five biggest spenders have committed $800.6 billion of 2026 capex (BBC). Tigay's phrase - the "show me phase" - is the regime: revenue growth no longer excuses spending; only the spending's payback does. The practical screen for your own list: operating cash flow minus capex, one line per holding, negative or positive.

2. The war's windfall math. Friday's Indian results quantified who the war pays. Fuel cracks at three to 3.7 times year-ago levels - historic highs, per RIL's release - and freight rates up 15 to 20 times turned Reliance's O2C EBITDA up 68% and Indian Oil's quarter into the best in its history. The mechanism: the war's cost lands on importers and consumers as a premium; the same premium lands on refiners' books as margin. India sits on both sides of that line - a crude importer paying the bill ($2 billion a year per dollar of crude) and a refining hub collecting the cracks. Watch the spread, not the headline price.

3. Gold's failed safety bid. Three tankers hit mines, a fourth claimed, in the world's most important oil chokepoint - and gold fell 3% to a one-year low of $3,901.83, down more than 25% from January's peak above $5,300. The safety bid went to US Treasuries instead: the ten-year yield has fallen from above 5.30% in early October to about 4.92%, the biggest monthly drop since late 2023. The lesson in the tape: in this war, the market's haven is the bond of the country fighting it, not the metal - because rate expectations (two Fed officials dissented for a hike this week) dominate gold's math more than fear does. Silver broke $50 for the first time since November 2025.

The builder's read of the Binance heist. The largest theft in crypto history - $6.3 billion, four times the record - was met with the industry's standard triage: freeze withdrawals, promise coverage, investigate. Binance can afford the promise; a smaller exchange cannot, and that asymmetry is the startup lesson. The gap in the market is verifiable solvency as a product feature: exchanges and fintechs that can prove - continuously, cryptographically - that customer money exists will take deposits from those that merely assert it. Insight: after every heist, the winners are not the loudest apologisers but the platforms whose proof-of-reserves is boring, frequent and third-party-checked.

Startup idea (one, as specified). Continuous proof-of-reserves as a service for Indian fintechs and crypto platforms. The product: a daily Merkle-tree attestation of customer liabilities matched against on-chain or custodian-verified assets, published to a public dashboard, with an API that regulators and partners can poll. Why now: the largest custody failure in history happened Thursday; every Indian exchange and wallet will be asked by its users, bankers and eventually its regulator how it proves solvency. First customers: the mid-size exchanges too small to absorb a loss and too proud to say so. What a good first year looks like: three paying platforms, one audit firm partnered, and a dashboard users actually check.
Opportunity watch. Nothing verified this cycle clears the bar for a specific grant, programme or competition deadline worth your time this week; the honest answer is an empty slot.

1. Demand was never the question - financing is. Intel's chief executive insists AI-driven demand is "extremely high"; his stock lost 28.6% anyway, because his guidance showed the cost of serving that demand. That is the whole of the AI race's new phase in one company: the five majors have committed $800.6 billion of 2026 spending, Amazon's free cash flow is $42.4 billion under water for the year, and the market has stopped paying for ambition on credit. Gene Goldman's verdict - "the real villain is AI spending" - and Tigay's - the "show me phase" - now set the terms for every model launch: show us who pays.

2. Radar. Nothing new shipped in the last 48 hours worth your install; the tape was the story. The more durable AI item of the day is a casualty: Reddit fell 26% after weak daily-user numbers, with Google's AI answers cited as eating its referral traffic - the first big consumer-internet print showing AI search replacing the click. If you build anything that lives on search traffic, that one print is the roadmap: the open web's referral economy is being repriced in real time. Roblox fell 20% on its own user numbers.

Friday's tape hands builders the cheapest lesson of the year: verification beats confidence. Intel's CEO was confident about demand; the market verified the funding instead. Do the same with your agents. When an agent handles a number that matters, give it an end-of-day source of truth - a final table, a filing, a settled price - not a live feed mid-session, and have it check that source before it writes. Then run the agent twice on anything load-bearing and diff the outputs: internal consistency is not correctness, because a model can be consistently wrong from a single stale read. The harness is boring; the failures it catches are not.

Check who funds the capex on one company you own. Saturday is money day, and this week's theme is the scoreboard. Steps: (1) pick one holding or watchlist name; (2) pull its latest quarterly results - the company's own release or BSE filing, not a summary; (3) find cash flow from operations and capital expenditure; (4) subtract: a positive number funds itself, a negative number burns; (5) write one dated line in a note: "funds itself" or "burns, and here is who pays." Time: fifteen minutes. What a good result looks like: one line per holding by next Saturday, so that when a results day like Friday hits, you already know which side of the tape your names are on.

Free cash flow is the cash a business generates after paying for the assets it needs to keep running: operating cash flow minus capital expenditure. It is the one number this week's market moved on, so it earns the deep treatment. The academic foundation is Michael Jensen's 1986 paper in the American Economic Review, "Agency Costs of Free Cash Flow, Corporate Finance, and Takeovers." Jensen defined free cash flow precisely - cash beyond what is needed to fund every positive-return project - and identified its danger: managers sitting on it tend to spend it on growth that serves them (empire, scale, prestige) rather than return it to owners. The mechanism is an agency problem: the people who decide the spending are not the people who own the cash. Jensen's prediction was that markets would discipline firms without credible payback for their spending - and that debt, which forces cash out the door, could paradoxically be a governance tool. Forty years on, the paper reads like Friday's playbook. Alphabet posted negative $9.07 billion of free cash flow in a quarter and lost $500 billion of value; Amazon is $42.4 billion under water over twelve months; Intel guided to spending the market refused to pre-fund and lost 28.6% in a day. Meanwhile Exxon, printing cash, touched a record. Applications beyond the tape: in insurance, float is the analogue - premiums held before claims are paid - and the same discipline question applies to whoever invests it; in product work, a feature's "free cash flow" is usage beyond its maintenance cost. The decision rule: before rewarding any company's growth story, ask who funds the capex - and what evidence would make them stop. Sixty-second recall, closed book: (1) Who formalised the free-cash-flow problem, and when? (2) What is the agency conflict at its heart? (3) What did Friday's market do to the biggest negative-FCF names? Answers: Michael Jensen, 1986; managers spend owners' cash on growth that serves managers; punished them - Alphabet, Amazon, Intel - while bidding the cash printers to records.

groups.heading: Term of the day: war-risk premium

blocks.html: The extra price buyers pay for a commodity or asset when conflict threatens its supply, above what peacetime fundamentals justify. It is measurable: Saxo Bank's read is a post-conflict oil range of $70-90 against a pre-war $60-70 - so the premium in today's $104-113 crude is roughly $30-40 a barrel. It is also broader than oil: the same premium shows up as 15-to-20-times freight rates, tanker insurance, and about $2 billion a year on India's import bill for every dollar it persists. The premium's behaviour is the tell for the war itself - it fills on escalation (Friday's mines) and leaks on diplomacy (this week's Qatari shuttle). When it goes to zero without a signed deal, distrust the calm.

The board goes into midterm week with its first holding 2.7% from target. Every live name on one board: terms in rows, nothing buried in prose. Conditional setups only - entry is a zone, never a market order. No orders are placed, ever; every call is scored by the standing rules in the ledger File. Every published setup stays until its target or its stop resolves it, with status kept honest daily.

blocks.html: Setup slots 2 to 5 are empty today. Nothing else cleared the verification bar into a midterm weekend; an empty slot is a result, not a gap. Friday's read, with per-share prices: HCLTech (Rs 1,428.00) added 1.2% and sits +3.3% against the cost-adjusted fill of Rs 1,382.13 (the Rs 1,378.00 worst fill plus 0.3% costs), target Rs 1,466.80 now 2.7% away; the level map is unchanged. Kotak Mahindra Bank (Rs 461.00) holds above its Rs 437.55 trigger - still a candidate, not a setup, and an empty slot is the honest entry. JSW Steel (Rs 1,245.00) holds above its floor and reclaim zone. ONGC (Rs 226.00) sits inside the Rs 218.50-238.75 coil as crude settles higher - the breakout above Rs 228 printed Tuesday was not held. Infosys (Rs 1,182.00) rose 3.4% as IT led Friday; the absorption thesis holds and the Rs 26 dividend record date lands Tuesday. Tech Mahindra stays shelved (price cap); its 1:1 bonus postal ballot is in voting, no record date set.

items.detail: A setup activates only if the zone fills before any prior-day trade at or below the stop.

items.title: Same-day zone and stop
items.detail: Unknowable from daily data: conservative scoring assumes the worst fill, then the stop.

items.title: Resolutions stay on record
items.detail: A setup leaves the board only when its target or stop resolves it; winners and losers both stay in the ledger.

blocks.html: Scoreboard first. Friday's watchlist: the results slate delivered records (Reliance, Bank of Baroda, Indian Oil); Jio's third session held above Rs 1,400 for the second day, adding 0.57% to Rs 1,431.20; and the foreign sellers of Thursday returned as buyers, Rs 3,599 crore provisional. All three resolved in the market's favour. The bigger read is Friday's decoupling: on the day Wall Street had its worst session since June and Asia fell apart, India rose - because its day was built on record profits, not on the AI trade. One day is not a regime, and midcaps and banks did fall. But the week's ledger shows a domestic-earnings bid absorbing a global scare, twice. New tests for the week ahead: (1) Tuesday's midterms - a 91-93% priced Democratic House meets a reported post-vote strike window; oil's premium is the live read on both. (2) EAAA's Monday listing tests whether Jio's afterglow lifts the shelf. (3) HCLTech's target at Rs 1,466.80 is 2.7% away - the board's first resolution is close enough to matter.

1. The midterms, Tuesday. America votes on 3 November: all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats (NBC's tracker); prediction markets price a Democratic House at 91-93%. The World Gold Council's framing: a Democratic Congress could restrict war funding - and the Wall Street Journal reports the strike window on Iran opens after the vote. Watch: the result, and oil Monday and Tuesday. Proves it wrong: the polls miss, or the premium leaks before a single result lands.

2. The Hormuz escalation ladder. Friday added three rungs at once: the war's first successful limpet-mine strike, a claimed Houthi hit on Ras Tanura, and the IRGC publicly mocking the "lanes cleared" claim. The cause chain: mines raise insurance, insurance raises freight, freight raises India's import bill. Watch: UKMTO advisories, tanker rates, and whether the Qatari shuttle produces an answer to the Vance letter. Proves it wrong: verified mine clearance and sustained tanker traffic without incident.

3. Binance's aftershock. The tell for contagion is boring plumbing: whether withdrawals resume and outflows stay orderly (FundStrat's Sean Farrell). If they do, $6.3 billion is an event - huge, but absorbed. Watch: Binance's withdrawal status and any second exchange halting. Proves it wrong: another platform freezes withdrawals.

One secondary report headlined Rs 25,548 crore (+40.6%), a figure that does not appear in the company's release.

Friday's Indian mover prices are BSE official closing prints via the exchange's quote data; the daily bhavcopy file was not reachable at build time. FII/DII figures are provisional exchange data (CNBC TV18) and may be revised. NSE surfaces were not accessed.
Jio Platforms' prices are BSE prints (close Rs 1,431.20); the NSE print is Rs 1,431.30. Broker targets quoted for Suzlon (Investec Rs 56, I-Sec Rs 55, UBS Rs 58) are the brokers' own published views.

Company claims - Suzlon's order book and deliveries, Jio's subscriber and ARPU figures, Binance's promise to cover losses, Intel's demand commentary - are the companies' own, labelled and dated as such. The North Korea attribution on the Binance theft is a blockchain intelligence firm's assessment carried by AP. X was not accessible for cross-checking.

Markets coverage is research, not advice: the setup board's levels are conditional research triggers with published invalidation and targets, not recommendations to buy or sell. No orders are placed; the ledger books results only on actual fills.

edition.title: Intel sinks 29%, India climbs on records
edition.fact: Saturday 31 October 2026, edition 26. Wall Street had its worst day since June - Intel fell 28.6% on weak guidance, the Nasdaq dropped 3.57% and the S&P 500 2.30% as the AI-spend reckoning spread - while the Sensex rose 308 points to 74,460 on a record Reliance quarter (profit Rs 29,550 crore, up 33.8%), record Bank of Baroda and Indian Oil results, and Jio Platforms' first results as a listed company; foreign investors returned, buying Rs 3,599 crore; three tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz - a fourth reported by Iran's army - in the war's first successful limpet-mine attack, and oil settled higher; and Binance confirmed a $6.3-billion theft, the largest crypto heist on record.
edition.intro: The 5-minute lead route is first; sections carry the detail. Yesterday this paper set Friday's watchlist: the results slate, Jio's third session, and whether foreign money would keep selling. All three verdicts are in the editor's read. The long read is Suzlon - the wind man's second life, timed to this week's record quarter and honest guidance cut.
